analysis.one_liner: Slashes payroll, income, corporate, and capital gains taxes for two years while canceling unspent stimulus money.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This Republican bill would have temporarily eliminated taxes on long-term capital gains and dividends, cut the employee share of Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes roughly in half, lowered corporate income tax rates, and cut the lowest income tax bracket from 10% to 5% — all for tax years 2009 and 2010. To pay for it, it would have canceled every dollar of unspent money from the 2009 stimulus law's discretionary programs. It was referred to the Ways and Means and Appropriations Committees on the day it was introduced and never moved again [S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, all workers would pay less payroll tax on their wages, self-employed people would see their payroll tax rates cut in half, and low-income taxpayers would pay a 5% rate on their first bracket of income. Investors — who are disproportionately higher-income households — would pay nothing on long-term capital gains and qualified dividends for two years, and corporations would see their top rates drop from 35% to 25% [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Halves the employee share of payroll taxes (Social Security from 6.2% to 3.1%, Medicare from 1.45% to 0.725%) for two years, and cuts the self-employment tax rates by the same proportion [S3].
Excludes all long-term capital gains and qualified dividend income from federal income tax for tax years 2009 and 2010 [S2][S3].
Cuts corporate marginal rates for 2009-2010 to 15% on income up to $50,000 and 25% above $75,000, down from rates up to 35%, and cuts the lowest individual bracket from 10% to 5% [S2][S3].
Offsets the cost by rescinding all unobligated discretionary appropriations from the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, the 2009 stimulus law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose tax revenue it does not currently collect, adding to the deficit unless matched by cuts; halved payroll tax payments would mean lower receipts for Social Security and Medicare; and the rescission clause would cancel unspent stimulus money that state and local governments, infrastructure projects, and other recovery programs were counting on [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury, Social Security/Medicare, and stimulus recipients

drawbacks.text: Rescinding all unobligated stimulus appropriations would cancel recovery spending — on infrastructure, state fiscal relief, and other programs — that had been enacted earlier in 2009 to counter the recession, potentially costing jobs those funds were meant to support [S2][S3].

Excluding all capital gains and dividends from tax primarily benefits households that own stocks and investment assets, which are concentrated among higher-income earners, so the largest dollar benefits would flow to the wealthiest taxpayers (general knowledge about the distribution of capital income).

Cutting the employee share of payroll taxes would reduce the dedicated revenue stream for Social Security and Medicare; the bill contains no provision to replace it, so either benefits would face pressure or general revenues would have to cover the gap (general knowledge about how payroll taxes fund those programs).

The bill includes no revenue offsets beyond the stimulus rescission, so its tax cuts would be financed by borrowing, adding to the federal deficit (general knowledge about how unpaid-for tax cuts work).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker-facing provisions — the halved employee payroll tax and the lower bottom bracket — are real and broad-based, and a payroll tax holiday is a standard recession-fighting tool. But the bill's largest benefits accrue to investors and corporations, its financing comes from canceling public recovery spending rather than from any structural offset, and halving Social Security and Medicare payroll receipts without a replacement creates a hole in programs that workers pay into their whole lives. It is a tax-cut package whose honest price tag sits with future taxpayers and with the programs the stimulus money was funding.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means and Appropriations Committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Broun of Georgia introduced the bill on November 18, 2009, with 39 Republican cosponsors, all from the House [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and the Appropriations Committee the same day [S1][S5].
No committee action, hearing, floor vote, or further step of any kind appears in the bill's action history; the last recorded action is the initial referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Recipients of unspent stimulus funds — including state and local governments and recovery projects — kept money the bill would have canceled, and the tax cuts were never enacted, so no new revenue hole was opened. Workers also never received the temporary payroll tax cut the bill promised.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; no markup, hearing, or vote was ever scheduled

against.name: House Appropriations Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the stimulus-rescission provision
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral

sides.party_line_note: All 40 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would cut corporate marginal rates from as high as 35% to 25% for two years, a direct tax saving for profitable companies. The cost falls on the Treasury and, through the stimulus rescission, on public recovery spending.

A two-year total tax exemption on long-term capital gains and qualified dividends benefits almost exclusively households that own stocks and other assets, which skew heavily toward higher incomes. Because those gains would otherwise be taxed, the benefit concentrates at the top.

industries.industry: State and local governments and stimulus-funded projects (infrastructure, energy, public programs)
industries.note: The bill rescinds every unobligated dollar of discretionary appropriations from the 2009 stimulus law, canceling recovery spending that had been allocated to stimulate the economy and support jobs.

The self-employment tax would be cut in half for two years, a direct benefit to people who work for themselves, alongside the corporate and individual rate cuts many small businesses also benefit from.
